title: How to Take a Week Off Without the Business Stopping
summary: A real week off, not a long weekend where you answered the phone eleven times. How to find out what only lives in your head and hand the rest off.
body_markdown:
When was the last time you took a real vacation? Not a long weekend where you answered the phone eleven times. A week where nothing routed through you.


You had to think about it, right?


You’re sitting in a position lots of other contractors face, too. You built a business where every decision passes through one person, because at the beginning that was the only way it could work. The problem is that nobody ever went back and changed it.


## Why everything ends up going through you


At three people, being the bottleneck is efficient. You know it from top to bottom: the client, the scope, the pricing, and the reason you framed that wall the way you did. Explaining it to someone takes longer than doing it.


So you keep it that way. And every month the amount of the business that exists only in your head grows a little.


Then a Tuesday comes where you're on a roof, a homeowner calls the office about a change, a sub texts asking which tile, and your supplier wants to know if the order is confirmed. All three of those people are waiting on the same person, and that person is holding a nail gun.


The reality is you became the single point of failure for a business that now has more moving parts than one person can hold.


## The test that tells you where you actually stand


Forget the week off for a second. Try a smaller version.


Take one day. Not a Saturday. A real Tuesday where you tell your crew and your clients you are unreachable until 4pm.


Then notice what breaks:


- How many people needed a decision only you could make
- How many of those decisions were genuinely hard
- How many were just a question about something already written down somewhere
- How many became a bigger problem because they waited


Most of what routes through you is not judgment. It's information that lives in your head and nowhere else. That's a much easier problem to solve than "I need to work less."


## Separate the two kinds of decisions


In the end, questions come in two camps. There are decisions only you can make, and there are decisions that only reach you because nobody else has the information.


1. **Only you can decide:** whether to take a job, what to price it at, whether to eat a cost, whether to keep a sub, how to handle a client who is genuinely unhappy.
2. **Anyone could decide, given the information:** which tile the client picked, whether the order was confirmed, what the schedule says for Thursday, what the scope covers for the trim.


The second list is where your week disappears. And every item on it is fixable without hiring anyone, because the fix is writing it down somewhere other people can look.


## Write down the four things people ask you most


You already know what they are. It's the same four questions every week, from the same categories of people.


Pick them off one at a time:


- **The scope question.** A written scope of work with the job, so a sub or a lead can answer it without calling you.[AI Documents](https://handoff.ai/ai-documents) can generate it from the estimate you already built.
- **The schedule question.** A real schedule somewhere both your crew and your clients can see, so "when are you coming back" stops being a phone call.
- **The client question.** A[client portal](https://handoff.ai/client-portal) where the homeowner can see their own project, their documents, and what they owe. A homeowner with somewhere to look calls less, and that means more time off for you.
- **The sub question.** Bids, scope, and agreements attached to the job instead of buried in your texts. The[Subcontractor Portal](https://handoff.ai/ai-subcontractor-portal) on Scale keeps that in one place, so a sub can check the agreement instead of asking you what you agreed on in April.


You aren’t handing anyone your judgment. You’re getting the reference material out of your head so your judgment is the only thing people actually need you for.


## Pick your second in command, even if it's part-time


At some point the information fix runs out and you need a person.


It doesn’t have to be a full-time operations hire. On a small shop it is usually the office spouse (insert this blog URL here when published[Blog / H2H Blog - What to Do When Your Business Partner Is Also Your Spouse](https://app.notion.com/p/Blog-H2H-Blog-What-to-Do-When-Your-Business-Partner-Is-Also-Your-Spouse-3d0fc39a5fa7802d8096eb360cf0749d?pvs=21) ), a lead carpenter who has been with you five years, or a part-time admin who handles the client-facing side two days a week.


What matters is that one other person can answer the ordinary questions and knows the boundary on the rest.


> Give them a dollar amount. Under this number, you decide. Over it, call me. Then let them make a few wrong calls without taking the authority back, because taking it back the first time it goes sideways teaches them to ask you about everything, which is exactly where you started.


## Do a dry run before you book anything


Don’t test this for the first time from an airport.


Take the Tuesday. Then a Thursday and a Friday together. Then a Monday through Wednesday. Each time, notice which question came to you anyway, and fix that one specific thing before the next attempt.


3-4 rounds of that and the week stops being theoretical. You’ll find out something useful either way: either the business can run for a few days without you, or you now know exactly which four things are stopping it.


## The reason this matters more than it sounds


A business that cannot run without you for a week is a business you cannot sell, cannot scale, and cannot get sick in.


That last one is the real risk. Nobody plans to be out for a month, and every contractor who has been out for a month found out the hard way what was only in their head. The work you do now to make a vacation possible is the same work that protects you when the choice is not yours.


And there's a version of this that is just about your life. You started this so you would not be working for someone else's schedule. Somewhere along the way you built a schedule that is harder to escape than any job you ever had. That's worth changing, and it's changeable.


> The goal is not a business that runs itself. It's a business where being unreachable for a few days is inconvenient instead of impossible.

## Other FAQs about getting vacation time as a remodeling business owner


**How long should a contractor be able to leave the business unattended?**


A few days is a reasonable first target for a two or three person shop. A full week is realistic once one other person can answer the ordinary questions and the reference material lives somewhere other than your head. Anyone telling you a small remodeling business should run itself for a month is describing a different kind of company.


**Who should you leave in charge if you don't have a project manager?**


Whoever already has the most context, which is usually the office spouse, a long-tenured lead carpenter, or a part-time admin. The title matters less than two things: they can answer the routine questions, and they know the dollar amount above which they call you. Both of those are decisions you make once.


**What do you tell clients when you're going to be unreachable?**


Tell them before you go, name the dates, and give them the person to contact instead. Homeowners handle a planned absence fine. What they don't handle is calling you on a Wednesday and getting nothing, because silence during their remodel is where an easygoing client turns into an anxious one.


**What if your crew genuinely can't work without you on site?**


Then the honest answer is you schedule around it for now, and start building toward a version where they can. Book the time off during a stretch between jobs, or during a phase a sub owns start to finish. That's a workaround rather than a fix, and the fix is the same as everything else here: someone else needs to be able to answer the question that only you can answer today.
